questions.stem: You are managing a £3.2 million refurbishment of a regional museum's galleries. Your stakeholder engagement plan schedules a one-hour weekly briefing with the sponsor, the museum director. After the second briefing she tells you she finds them too detailed and would prefer to hear from you only when she has a decision to make or a risk is heading her way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the weekly briefings but shorten them to thirty minutes, cutting the detail down to a one-page summary for her.
options.rationale: It responds to the format complaint but not to what she actually asked for. Candidates pick it because it feels like a compromise, yet it still spends her time on a meeting she has said she does not need.

options.text: Explain that weekly sponsor briefings form part of the approved plan, and continue holding them with her as scheduled.
options.rationale: It treats the plan as a commitment to the document rather than to the person. A sponsor's stated engagement preference is exactly the information the plan should be revised on.

options.text: Stop the briefings and copy her on the weekly status report so that she can pick out anything she needs to act on.
options.rationale: It moves the burden of spotting what matters onto her, which is the opposite of her request. Candidates choose it because it reduces meetings, but it buries her decisions inside a report she did not ask for.

options.text: Agree with her what counts as a decision or risk she must hear about, and update the engagement plan to match.
options.rationale: The plan exists to serve the stakeholder's needs, and she has just told you what they are. Agreeing the triggers turns her preference into something you can apply consistently, and recording it keeps the plan current.

questions.explanation: An engagement plan is a working hypothesis about how each stakeholder wants to be involved, and the stakeholder's own feedback is the best evidence for revising it. When a key stakeholder asks for less contact, the task is to agree precisely what must still reach them — the triggers and thresholds — so that reducing contact does not reduce their control. A plan defended against the stakeholder it was written for has stopped being an engagement plan.
questions.mindset: Tailor engagement to how each stakeholder wants to be involved, and revise the plan when they tell you.

questions.stem: On a rail signalling upgrade, the main installation contractor's new engagement lead asks you for a copy of your stakeholder register so their team can plan site communications with the same people. Your register includes contact details and roles, but also your candid assessments of each stakeholder's attitude and influence, including notes such as 'likely to resist possession weekends'. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send the full register so that the contractor works from the same picture as you, and ask them in writing to treat the contents as confidential.
options.rationale: A confidentiality request does not control what happens once candid notes sit in another organisation's systems. Candidates choose it to keep both parties aligned, but alignment does not require sharing judgements about named people.

options.text: Share a version holding roles, contacts and communication needs, and keep the attitude and influence assessments restricted to the project team.
options.rationale: The contractor has a legitimate need for who to contact and how, and no need for your judgements about individuals. Splitting the register meets the need without exposing assessments that would damage relationships if they circulated.

options.text: Decline the request and offer to pass the contractor whichever individual stakeholder contacts their team needs, case by case as they arise.
options.rationale: Withholding everything makes you a bottleneck for routine contacts the contractor needs to do its job, and treats a reasonable coordination request as a threat. Only part of the register is the problem.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to decide whether the contractor may see the register, given that it names and assesses senior people in the client organisation.
options.rationale: The register is a project document you maintain, and deciding how to share it is within your remit. Escalating spends the sponsor's time on a decision you can make yourself with a sensible split of the content.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis holds two kinds of information: what others need in order to engage people, such as names, roles and preferred channels, and the team's private judgements about attitude and influence. The first can be shared widely; the second is sensitive and can harm relationships if seen by the people it describes. Structure the register so the shareable and sensitive parts can be separated, and decide distribution on need to know.
questions.mindset: Share what others need to engage stakeholders, and protect your private judgements about them.

questions.stem: Your team is building a stock-ordering app for 640 bakery franchisees. Because the whole network cannot attend sprint reviews, you recruited a panel of eight franchisees who volunteered. Six sprints in, the panel rates every increment highly. You notice that all eight run high-volume city-centre shops and had asked to be early adopters. Release to the wider network is three sprints away. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the panel, which has built useful continuity with the team, and run a wider survey of franchisees after the first release goes live.
options.rationale: Continuity is real, but it is being bought with a blind spot. Candidates choose it to protect a working arrangement, and it postpones the unrepresented view until after release, when it costs most to act on.

options.text: Bring franchisees from smaller and rural outlets into the panel now, chosen to reflect the network rather than by volunteering.
options.rationale: The panel's approval is only evidence for the franchisees it represents. Changing its make-up while three sprints remain lets the backlog absorb what smaller outlets need before release fixes the design in front of them.

options.text: Ask the current panel members to gather feedback from neighbouring franchisees before each review and report it on their behalf.
options.rationale: Second-hand feedback relayed by enthusiastic city-centre owners carries their framing. It looks like broadening the input, but the people missing from the room are still missing.

options.text: Present the panel's ratings to the sponsor with a clear note that they come from high-volume shops, and let the sponsor judge the risk.
options.rationale: Disclosing the bias is honest, but it hands over a problem you can fix yourself to someone who cannot fix it more easily. Candidates pick it for transparency, and the gap in the evidence stays open.

questions.explanation: When a large stakeholder group is represented by a sample, the sample's feedback speaks only for the segments it contains. Volunteers are self-selected and usually the most enthusiastic, so positive feedback from a volunteer panel is weak evidence about the whole population. Check the sample against the segments that will be affected, and correct it while there is still time for what they say to change the product.
questions.mindset: Ask whose view a piece of feedback represents before treating it as everyone's.

questions.stem: Your organisation is developing a telematics service for its tractors, with the hardware on a predictive plan and the software built in sprints. The head of sales is the project's most enthusiastic supporter and wants to announce a launch month at a dealer conference in three weeks to build orders. The hardware certification date is not yet baselined, and the team's best estimate spans four months. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Give the head of sales the latest month in the four-month range, so that whatever is announced is unlikely to be missed by the project.
options.rationale: A padded date is still a public commitment made before the plan supports it, and dealers will plan stock around it. Candidates choose it as the safe option, but it fixes an external expectation on an unbaselined estimate.

options.text: Work with the head of sales on what can be announced now, such as features and a pilot sign-up, leaving the date until baseline.
options.rationale: It keeps the supporter's energy pointed at the project while protecting the one thing that cannot yet be promised. Giving him something real to announce makes the conversation about how he can help, not whether he may.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to instruct the head of sales not to mention launch timing at the conference until the hardware date is baselined.
options.rationale: It may stop the announcement, but it turns your strongest supporter into someone overruled on his own territory. Candidates pick it as proper escalation; the cost is the relationship the project relies on.

options.text: Share the full four-month range and its assumptions, so that the head of sales can make an informed decision about what to tell dealers.
options.rationale: Transparency is right, but handing the decision to the person most motivated to announce early invites the most optimistic reading of the range. It informs him without engaging him on what the project needs.

questions.explanation: Supportive stakeholders need managing as much as resistant ones, because enthusiasm can create commitments the project cannot keep. The aim is to channel their support toward actions that help rather than to suppress it: find what they can legitimately do now, and agree the conditions under which the rest becomes possible. Restraining a champion by authority costs the support; arming them with an uncertain figure costs the credibility.
questions.mindset: Give an enthusiastic supporter something useful to do with their support, not just a reason to wait.

questions.stem: You are replacing the laboratory information system at a pharmaceutical quality-control site. The lab manager is the only person who understands several of the release-testing workflows, and she has cancelled three of the four two-hour requirements workshops scheduled with her, citing batch release deadlines. Her deputy says she supports the project but cannot leave the lab for long. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the site director to formally protect two hours of her time each week so that the scheduled workshops can go ahead as planned.
options.rationale: It treats a scheduling mismatch as a commitment problem and puts her in the position of being instructed by her director. Candidates reach for it to secure the time; it secures attendance at the cost of goodwill.

options.text: Run the remaining workshops with her deputy instead, and ask the lab manager to review the resulting requirements in writing.
options.rationale: The deputy does not hold the knowledge that makes her essential, and a written review of second-hand requirements is the hardest way to spot what is missing. It looks efficient but loses the content.

options.text: Move the cancelled workshops to after the batch release peak, and adjust the requirements timeline to accommodate the delay.
options.rationale: Batch release pressure at a quality-control site recurs, so waiting for a quiet period may mean waiting indefinitely. Candidates choose it out of respect for her workload, and it gives away schedule for nothing.

options.text: Offer shorter sessions held in the lab at times she chooses, with draft workflow notes sent beforehand for her to correct.
options.rationale: She is willing but constrained, so the format is the problem, not the person. Going to her and doing the drafting yourself turns her scarce time into correction, which is the part only she can do.

questions.explanation: When a supportive stakeholder cannot engage in the way the plan assumed, change the mechanism rather than pressing the stakeholder. Go to where they work, reduce the time each contact needs, and prepare material so their effort goes on what only they can contribute. An engagement method is a means of getting the stakeholder's input, and a method the stakeholder cannot use is the wrong method.
questions.mindset: Fit the engagement to the stakeholder's working reality rather than asking them to fit the plan.

questions.stem: A credit union's agile team is rebuilding its loan application journey. The compliance officer has started insisting that every user story be sent to her for review before it enters a sprint, including stories about button colours and page layout. Refinement is backing up and the product owner is frustrated. She has not said what prompted the request. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Agree with the product owner which stories carry regulatory content, and route only those to her for review before sprint planning.
options.rationale: It is probably close to where things end up, but deciding the filter without her assumes you know what she considers regulatory. Candidates choose it because it is efficient; it designs around her rather than with her.

options.text: Invite her to attend backlog refinement every week so that she can review the stories as they are written rather than afterwards.
options.rationale: It gives her more access before anyone knows why she wants it, which may make the bottleneck permanent. Candidates pick it as inclusive, but it accepts her method without testing her need.

options.text: Meet the compliance officer to find out what risk or past event she is trying to guard against with the reviews.
options.rationale: Her request is a solution to a concern she has not named. Until you know whether it was an audit finding, a past incident or uncertainty about the product, any narrowing of her role may miss the thing she needs controlled.

options.text: Explain that design and layout stories carry no compliance risk, and ask her to limit her review to stories about lending rules.
options.rationale: Consumer lending rules can reach presentation, such as how rates and fees are displayed, so the claim may be wrong. Telling a compliance officer what falls within her remit is the quickest way to harden her position.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder imposes a control that seems disproportionate, the request is usually a proxy for a concern they have not stated. Find the underlying interest before negotiating the mechanism, because the right response depends on it: an audit finding, a past incident and a lack of trust each call for different engagement. Negotiating positions before understanding interests tends to produce either capitulation or conflict.
questions.mindset: Understand the concern behind a stakeholder's demand before deciding how to meet it.

questions.stem: You are managing a £14 million new-build secondary school. Your engagement plan promised the heads of science, art and design technology a review of the final classroom layouts before design sign-off. While you were on leave, the design lead submitted the layouts early to meet the architect's deadline, skipping that review, and the client's estates board approved them yesterday. The three heads have not yet noticed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the three heads now that the promised review was missed, show them the approved layouts, and route any changes they need through change control.
options.rationale: A broken engagement commitment does least damage when the stakeholders hear it from you first. The approval stands, so change control is the honest route for what they still need, and it keeps the board's decision intact.

options.text: Hold the promised review this month as planned, and take any comments the heads raise forward as minor design refinements without reopening the approval.
options.rationale: It keeps the form of the promise but not its substance, and slipping changes past an approved design is a scope decision you cannot make quietly. Candidates choose it to honour the plan; it hides the miss instead of owning it.

options.text: Ask the estates board to withdraw its approval so that the heads' review can take place before design sign-off, as the plan originally committed.
options.rationale: It restores the sequence at the cost of the architect's programme and the board's time, before anyone knows whether the heads want changes at all. Candidates pick it as the principled fix; it is disproportionate to an unknown gap.

options.text: Check the approved layouts against the requirements the heads gave at the briefing stage, and contact them only if the check finds a gap.
options.rationale: It decides on the heads' behalf whether their review mattered, which is the judgement the promise gave to them. Candidates choose it as efficient, and if they later find out, the lost trust costs more than the meeting.

questions.explanation: An engagement plan is a set of promises to stakeholders, and when one is broken the damage depends mainly on who tells them and when. Disclose the miss promptly and directly, explain what can still change and through which route, and let the stakeholders judge its importance for themselves. Concealing a broken commitment, or quietly working around the approval it bypassed, turns a process slip into a breach of trust.
questions.mindset: When you break a promise to a stakeholder, make sure they hear it from you first.

questions.stem: Eight months into a council's housing repairs system replacement, your stakeholder register still records the head of tenant services as resistant, based on her objections at the initiation meeting. The team has since kept contact with her to a minimum. A colleague mentions that her objection was to a self-service booking feature, which the steering group dropped in month three. Her team's sign-off is needed for the next release. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet her to hear her current view of the project and what her team needs from the next release, then update the register.
options.rationale: The label rests on one meeting eight months ago and a colleague's report. Only she can tell you where she stands now, and her team's sign-off makes it worth asking directly before the release depends on it.

options.text: Change her assessment to neutral now that her original objection no longer applies, and include her in the release planning.
options.rationale: It replaces one unverified assessment with another. Candidates choose it because the evidence points that way, but a second-hand account of why she objected is not her current position.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to brief her on the dropped feature before the release, so that she hears the news from someone senior.
options.rationale: A senior briefing may help, but it assumes the dropped feature is all that matters to her. Candidates pick it to show respect; it still has the project talking at her rather than listening.

options.text: Send her a summary of scope changes since initiation, highlighting the removal of self-service booking, and invite her questions.
options.rationale: A written summary corrects her information but tells you nothing about her view. Candidates choose it as a low-cost update, and it continues the minimal contact that let the label go stale.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder's attitude in the register is an observation with a date on it, not a fixed trait. Assessments drift as the project changes, and a label that drives behaviour, such as minimising contact, can outlive the cause that justified it. Re-assess through direct engagement rather than inference, especially before a point at which that stakeholder's support will be needed.
questions.mindset: Treat a stakeholder assessment as dated evidence and check it directly before relying on it.

questions.stem: On a travel company's booking platform, the regional sales director has started attending the team's daily stand-up. Each morning he raises new requests from his key accounts and asks developers to fit them in that day. Two developers have quietly done so, and the sprint goal is slipping. He is a significant stakeholder whose accounts generate a third of revenue. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the product owner to set up a regular slot with him to take his requests into the backlog for prioritisation.
options.rationale: His requests are legitimate input, and the product owner is the person who weighs them against everything else. Giving him a reliable route into the backlog removes his reason to bypass it.

options.text: Ask him to stop attending the stand-up, explaining that it is a planning meeting for the development team only.
options.rationale: It is right about the stand-up's purpose, but it closes the door he is using without opening another. Candidates choose it to protect the team; a significant stakeholder with no channel will find a new workaround.

options.text: Let him keep attending, but ask the developers to log his requests and raise them at the next sprint planning.
options.rationale: It stops work entering the sprint but leaves developers fielding a senior director's requests every morning. Candidates pick it as a compromise; it keeps the product owner out of the decision.

options.text: Meet him to agree that urgent account requests may enter the sprint if they come with a revenue figure attached.
options.rationale: It sets a prioritisation rule that is the product owner's to set, and it makes the sprint negotiable by whoever brings a number. Candidates choose it to be businesslike; it undermines the sprint goal.

questions.explanation: In agile delivery, stakeholder requests reach the team through the backlog, and the product owner owns the decision about their priority. When an important stakeholder routes around that, the fix is to give them a dependable channel to the owner rather than simply blocking the route they found. Stakeholders bypass a process when it does not seem to serve them.
questions.mindset: Give stakeholders a working route to the decision owner so they have no reason to go around it.

questions.stem: You are planning consultation with academic staff for a university's new coursework submission system. Your engagement plan relies on an online survey, but the first one drew a 9% response. Heads of department tell you staff have been surveyed by five other projects this term and are ignoring them. Each department holds a monthly staff meeting. Design decisions need staff input within six weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reissue a much shorter version of the survey, with a reminder from the pro-vice-chancellor encouraging staff to respond.
options.rationale: A shorter survey with senior backing addresses effort and authority, but not the fatigue that heads of department identified. Candidates choose it because it fixes the instrument, and the instrument was not the problem.

options.text: Ask the five other projects to pause their surveys for six weeks so that yours can be completed while design is still open.
options.rationale: It asks other projects to bear your cost, and you have no authority to impose it. Candidates pick it because it removes the competition, but it solves your problem by creating theirs.

options.text: Replace the survey with short agenda slots at departmental staff meetings, accepting that the input will be less uniform.
options.rationale: It moves the consultation to a forum staff already attend and stops adding to the fatigue. The trade is structured data for real engagement, which is the right trade when the structured route has failed.

options.text: Proceed with the 9% response, weighting the results by department so that they better reflect the views of all academic staff.
options.rationale: Weighting corrects for who answered, not for the views of those who did not. Candidates choose it as a statistical fix, and it builds design decisions on the minority who still answer surveys.

questions.explanation: Engagement methods compete for stakeholders' limited attention, and when a group is saturated, adding more requests of the same kind produces less. Use channels the stakeholders already attend, even if the input is less tidy, and treat a low response as information about the method rather than about the stakeholders' interest. The best engagement method is the one stakeholders will actually use.
questions.mindset: Meet stakeholders in the forums they already use rather than adding another claim on their attention.

questions.stem: A logistics firm's agile team will demonstrate an automated shift-allocation feature at tomorrow's sprint review, which the operations director and about thirty depot staff attend. While preparing, you realise the feature removes the overtime-approval task that the four night-shift supervisors currently perform, and nobody has told them. Two of them will be at the review. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the feature back from tomorrow's demonstration and brief the supervisors properly at a meeting during the next sprint.
options.rationale: It avoids the public surprise by delaying both the feedback the review exists to collect and the conversation the supervisors are owed. Candidates choose it as cautious; it treats the demonstration as the problem when the problem is that they have not been told.

options.text: Demonstrate the feature as planned and open the floor for questions, so that the supervisors hear about the change alongside everyone else.
options.rationale: Treating everyone equally sounds fair, but the supervisors are not affected equally: they would learn of a loss of responsibility in public. Candidates pick it for transparency, and it turns their first reaction into a scene at the review.

options.text: Email the four supervisors this evening with a written summary of the feature and how it changes their overtime-approval duties.
options.rationale: It informs them before the review, which is better than nothing, but a written notice the night before tells them about the change without hearing them. Candidates choose it because it is quick; it delivers news that needs a conversation through a channel that cannot hold one.

options.text: Speak to the four night-shift supervisors today, before the review, to explain the change and hear their concerns about it.
options.rationale: People affected by a change to their role should hear it privately and first, not discover it in a room of thirty colleagues. There is still a day to do that, and listening now gives their concerns a route other than the review itself.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders whose role or interests are directly affected by a change should hear about it before any public forum, and in a format that lets them respond. Reviews and demonstrations are for feedback on the product, and they go badly when they double as the moment someone learns their job has changed. When the window to tell people first is short, use it rather than waiting for a better one.
questions.mindset: Make sure the people most affected by a change hear it first and privately, not in a public demonstration.

questions.stem: On a hospital pharmacy automation project, your business analyst has completed the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix for all 22 identified stakeholders. She has set the desired engagement level for every one of them to 'leading', and her proposed engagement plan would take roughly a third of your time each week. The sponsor has approved a budget line for engagement but has not reviewed the plan's detail. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Approve the plan as written, since stronger engagement across all 22 stakeholders lowers the risk of resistance, and delegate the extra meetings to the analyst.
options.rationale: It assumes more engagement is always better. Candidates choose it because resistance is a real risk, but the effort is real too, and twenty-two stakeholders all trying to lead would compete to steer the same project.

options.text: Keep 'leading' as the long-term aspiration for all 22, but phase the engagement activities so that the highest-power stakeholders are covered first.
options.rationale: Prioritising by power is sensible, which is why candidates pick it, but it keeps the flawed target and only changes the order of work towards it. The plan still aims to turn every stakeholder into a driver of the project.

options.text: Revisit each stakeholder's desired level with her, based on what the project needs from that person, and target effort at the gaps that matter.
options.rationale: The desired level is a statement of what the project needs from a particular stakeholder, and most of the 22 do not need to drive the work. Setting levels individually shrinks the plan to the gaps worth closing and frees the time to close them properly.

options.text: Reduce the plan's effort by moving every stakeholder's desired level down to 'supportive', which still secures backing without asking them to drive the work.
options.rationale: It corrects one blanket rule with another. Candidates choose it as a pragmatic compromise, yet the sponsor and the chief pharmacist may genuinely need to lead, while others only need to be aware. The fault was the uniformity, not the level chosen.

questions.explanation: Desired engagement levels are set stakeholder by stakeholder, from what the project needs each person to do, and the plan's effort goes on the gaps between current and desired levels that matter most. A uniform target, high or low, is a sign that the analysis has not been done. Engagement costs the time of the project and of the stakeholders, so the aim is the right level for each, not the highest level for all.
questions.mindset: Set the engagement you need from each stakeholder, rather than the most engagement you can get from all of them.

questions.stem: Your company funds an open-source data-visualisation library, and you lead the agile team that maintains it. The next major release changes the API in ways that will break code in many dependent projects. When the change surfaced in the public issue tracker, external contributors and maintainers of dependent projects reacted angrily, saying they had no warning. None is under contract to you, but the library's adoption depends on them. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Publish the reasoning for the change and a proposed migration path, and open a fixed comment period before the API design is finalised.
options.rationale: The complaint is that the decision was made out of their sight. Putting the reasoning and the migration path in the open while the design can still move gives them a voice that counts, which is the only lever you have with stakeholders who are not under contract.

options.text: Invite maintainers of the most-used dependent projects to try early builds of the new API and feed back during the next few iterations.
options.rationale: These are the people who carry the cost of the change. Early builds let them find the breakage themselves while the team can still respond, and turn the loudest critics into contributors to the solution.

options.text: Lock the issue thread to stop the discussion escalating, and post a single statement confirming the decision, the rationale and the release date.
options.rationale: It restores order in the tracker, which is why candidates choose it, but it confirms the community's complaint that they have no say. Volunteers who feel shut out stop contributing and start forking.

options.text: Keep the breaking change as designed but delay the release by two quarters, so that dependent projects have longer to adjust their code before it lands.
options.rationale: More time addresses the cost of migrating but not the exclusion that caused the anger. Candidates pick it as a generous concession; dependent maintainers still have no influence over a design they will have to live with.

options.text: Survey the library's registered users by email to measure how many would be affected before deciding whether to respond in the issue tracker.
options.rationale: Data on impact is useful, but the affected stakeholders have already identified themselves and the conversation is happening now in the tracker. Candidates choose it to be evidence-led; it delays engagement while the reaction hardens.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders who are not bound by contract engage voluntarily, so the project's main lever with them is a visible, genuine say in decisions that affect them. Open the reasoning, involve those who bear the cost while the design can still change, and use the channels where they already are. Controlling the conversation, or offering concessions without influence, leaves the original grievance in place.
questions.mindset: With stakeholders you cannot instruct, a visible say in the decision is the engagement.

questions.stem: You are managing the digitisation of a national archive's map collection on a predictive plan. Your engagement plan treats the chief archivist as the key decision-maker, and you brief her before each design gate. Twice she has rejected a proposal after taking it to an advisory panel of historians that meets quarterly and does not appear in your register. She says she will not decide such matters without the panel. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Add the advisory panel to the stakeholder register and analysis, recording how it shapes the chief archivist's design decisions.
options.rationale: The panel is a stakeholder with real influence over your outcomes, exercised through someone else. Recording it, and the relationship, corrects an analysis that has been planning engagement around only half of the decision.

options.text: Ask the chief archivist to arrange for you to present upcoming design proposals to the panel, timed around its quarterly meetings.
options.rationale: It works with her stated practice rather than against it, and through her rather than around her. Planning gates around the panel's calendar means proposals reach it before the decision rather than after a rejection.

options.text: Ask the chief archivist to agree a deadline after which design decisions will be taken without the panel's input if it has not yet met.
options.rationale: It protects the schedule, which is why candidates choose it, but it asks her to set aside a practice she has just said she will keep. Pressing a decision-maker to drop her advisers tends to harden the practice rather than shorten it.

options.text: Raise the two rejections with the sponsor as an issue, asking for the chief archivist's decision rights over the design to be confirmed in writing.
options.rationale: Her decision rights are not in doubt: she is exercising them, and choosing to take advice first. Candidates pick it to secure clarity, but it treats a stakeholder's legitimate way of deciding as a governance failure.

options.text: Give the chief archivist fuller technical documentation with each proposal, so that she can answer the panel's questions without needing to defer to it.
options.rationale: It assumes she consults the panel because she lacks information, when she has said it is how she decides. Candidates choose it as better preparation; it improves the briefing for the wrong audience.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder influence often runs through relationships, so a decision-maker may depend on advisers who never appear in project meetings. When decisions keep turning on people outside the analysis, add them to it and plan engagement around how the decision is actually made, working with the decision-maker's process rather than trying to shorten it. The formal decision-maker and the effective influencers are both stakeholders.
questions.mindset: Engage the people who shape a decision, not only the person who announces it.

questions.stem: Six months into a hybrid programme moving a dental group's 40 practices to electronic patient records, the sponsor asks how you know the stakeholder engagement plan is working. Your monthly report lists activities completed: 12 newsletters issued, 31 practice visits made and 4 webinars held. Practice managers and lead dentists are the stakeholders whose support the rollout depends on. Which two measures would give the sponsor the best evidence?

options.text: The change in each key stakeholder's assessed engagement level since the last review, compared with the desired level set in the plan.
options.rationale: This measures the thing the plan is for: movement of named stakeholders towards the engagement the programme needs. It shows where the gap is closing and where it is not, which is what the sponsor can act on.

options.text: Whether practice managers are doing what the rollout needs from them, such as nominating super-users and attending readiness reviews on time.
options.rationale: Behaviour is the most direct evidence of engagement. A practice manager who nominates super-users on time is supporting the rollout, whatever they say in a survey, and one who does not is a gap the plan should address.

options.text: The open and click-through rates of the newsletters, broken down by role, to show how far the programme's messages are reaching each group.
options.rationale: It is more refined than a count of newsletters, which is why candidates choose it, but it still measures reach. Reading a message is not the same as supporting the change it describes.

options.text: The number of practices visited against the visiting schedule in the plan, showing that the engagement activities are being delivered on time.
options.rationale: It measures whether the programme did what it planned, not how stakeholders responded. Candidates pick it because plan compliance is easy to evidence; a visit on schedule can still leave a practice opposed.

options.text: A survey of the programme team asking how well they think stakeholder relationships are going across the 40 practices, repeated each quarter.
options.rationale: It asks the people delivering the engagement to judge its success. Candidates choose it as a practical pulse check; it captures the team's perception of stakeholders rather than evidence from them.

questions.explanation: The effectiveness of stakeholder engagement is shown by stakeholders' engagement and behaviour, not by the volume of activity aimed at them. Activity counts and reach figures describe inputs; reassessed engagement levels against the desired levels, and the actions stakeholders take when the project needs them, describe outcomes. Reporting inputs as if they were outcomes makes a plan look successful while gaps stay open.
questions.mindset: Judge engagement by what stakeholders do, not by how much the project did to them.

questions.stem: You are identifying stakeholders for a predictive project to merge two county councils' planning departments. Match each identification gap to the technique most likely to close it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: You suspect there are affected groups inside the two departments that nobody on the project team has worked with before.
You need to be sure that every external body with a statutory right to be consulted on planning changes is included.
A neighbouring council completed a similar merger three years ago, and you want to learn from whom they overlooked.

options.text: Ask each stakeholder already identified who else will be affected or should be involved
options.rationale: People inside the departments know their own dependencies and neighbours far better than the project team does. Asking each identified stakeholder who else matters reaches groups the team cannot see from outside.

options.text: Review the legislation, regulations and agreements that govern planning services
options.rationale: Statutory consultees are defined by law and agreements, not by anyone's memory. Working from the governing documents is the only way to be confident the list is complete.

options.text: Review the earlier merger's stakeholder register and lessons learned
options.rationale: Historical records of a comparable project show who was identified, and lessons learned often record who was found late. That is exactly the knowledge the gap calls for.

options.text: Run a brainstorming session with the project team to list everyone they can think of
options.rationale: Not used. Brainstorming draws on what the team already knows, and each gap here is defined by something the team does not know. It is a good starting point for identification, not a fix for its blind spots.

questions.explanation: Each stakeholder identification technique draws on a different source of knowledge, so the right one depends on where the gap lies. People already identified know their own networks; governing documents define who has rights; records of similar projects show who was missed before. The project team's own knowledge is the starting point, and its limits are the reason the other techniques exist.
questions.mindset: Choose an identification technique for the knowledge it reaches that the team does not already have.

questions.stem: On a retail bank's agile mobile-app team, several stakeholders have asked how they can stay involved. Match each request to the mechanism that best serves it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The head of branch operations wants to try the latest working features and say whether they suit branch staff.
The marketing director wants a loyalty feature delivered before a campaign launch, ahead of other planned work.
The risk manager wants to see at any time what the team is working on, without interrupting anyone.

options.text: Attend the sprint review
options.rationale: The sprint review exists to inspect working software with stakeholders and gather their feedback. Trying the features and judging fit for branch staff is precisely its purpose.

options.text: Take the request to the product owner for backlog prioritisation
options.rationale: Moving one feature ahead of others is a priority decision, and the product owner owns it. Routing the request there gets it weighed against everything else rather than negotiated with individual developers.

options.text: Use the team's visible task board
options.rationale: An information radiator shows current work to anyone who looks, at any time, without a meeting or a question. It meets a need for visibility without costing the team any attention.

options.text: Attend the team's daily stand-up
options.rationale: Not used. The stand-up is for the developers to plan their next day's work. Stakeholder attendance tends to turn it into a status report, and none of the three needs it.

questions.explanation: Agile delivery gives stakeholders specific routes in: reviews for feedback on working product, the product owner for priorities, and visible boards for transparency. Matching each need to its route keeps stakeholders properly involved while protecting the team's working events. When stakeholders use a route meant for something else, it is usually because nobody showed them the right one.
questions.mindset: Point each stakeholder need to the route built for it, so engagement strengthens the process rather than bypassing it.

questions.stem: Your engagement assessment matrix for a hybrid airport baggage-system upgrade shows a gap between current and desired engagement for three stakeholders. Complete each sentence with the first step that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The airline operators' committee is assessed as unaware of the project, although its members' check-in processes will change. The first step is to
The baggage handlers' shift manager is assessed as resistant, and the reason for the resistance has not been recorded. The first step is to
The commercial director is assessed as leading although the plan needs her only to be supportive, and she has begun directing the contractor. The first step is to

options.text: brief them on the project and on what it will change in their operations
options.rationale: A stakeholder cannot support or resist something they do not know about. Closing an unawareness gap starts with telling them what the project is and how it affects them, before asking anything of them.

options.text: find out what lies behind the resistance before choosing how to respond
options.rationale: Resistance has causes, and the response depends on which one it is: a workload fear, a safety concern and a past grievance each need something different. With the reason unrecorded, finding it out comes first.

options.text: agree with her and the sponsor the role the project needs her to play
options.rationale: Over-engagement is a gap too. Directing the contractor cuts across the project's lines of authority, and agreeing her role with her and the sponsor channels her energy without rejecting her support.

options.text: invite them onto the steering group so that their views shape decisions
options.rationale: Not used. A seat on the steering group can raise a supportive stakeholder's influence, but it is premature for someone unaware, unexplained for someone resistant, and the opposite of what an over-engaged stakeholder needs.

questions.explanation: A gap between current and desired engagement is closed by a step chosen for its direction and cause. Unaware stakeholders need information first, resistant ones need their reasons understood before any response, and stakeholders engaged beyond what the project needs need a clearly agreed role. Treating every gap as a need for more involvement misreads half of them.
questions.mindset: Read the direction and cause of an engagement gap before deciding how to close it.

questions.stem: Your team prioritises stakeholders for a ferry-terminal expansion using a weighted score: power counts 60% and interest 40%, each rated from 1 to 5. The harbour authority is rated power 5, interest 3. The local fishing cooperative is rated power 2, interest 5. Stakeholders scoring 3.5 or above are assigned a named engagement owner. Work out each score and apply the threshold.

blanks.label: Weighted score for the harbour authority, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Power 5 × 0.6 = 3.0 and interest 3 × 0.4 = 1.2, so the score is 3.0 + 1.2 = 4.2, comfortably above the 3.5 threshold.

blanks.label: Weighted score for the fishing cooperative, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Power 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 and interest 5 × 0.4 = 2.0, so the score is 1.2 + 2.0 = 3.2. Its high interest is not enough to offset low power under these weights.

blanks.label: Does the fishing cooperative qualify for a named engagement owner — yes or no
blanks.rationale: 3.2 is below the 3.5 threshold, so the rule does not assign an owner. It still needs keeping informed: a highly interested group with low formal power can gain influence quickly if it feels ignored.

questions.explanation: A weighted score ranks stakeholders by the attributes the team has chosen to value, so the weights are a judgement about what matters and should be stated alongside the result. Applying a threshold gives consistency, but falling below it decides the intensity of engagement, not whether a stakeholder is engaged at all. Highly interested stakeholders with little formal power still need a planned channel.
questions.mindset: Use a prioritisation score to allocate effort, and remember it says nothing about who can be ignored.

questions.stem: A charity's agile team is building a volunteer-scheduling app. The volunteer network coordinator attends every sprint review, sends detailed feedback afterwards and keeps asking for more involvement. She holds no budget, cannot change scope and plays no part in decisions; the product owner decides priorities. Select the quadrant of the power–interest grid where she belongs.

graphic.title: Power–interest grid with four quadrants and their engagement strategies
graphic.caption: Select a quadrant. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: High power, low interest — keep satisfied
regions.rationale: This places her on the wrong side of both axes. She has shown sustained interest and holds none of the levers that make a stakeholder powerful, such as budget, scope or decision rights.

regions.label: High power, high interest — manage closely
regions.rationale: The most common error: reading the intensity of her engagement as power. Her interest is high, but frequent, detailed feedback does not give her authority over budget, scope or priorities.

regions.label: Low power, low interest — monitor
regions.rationale: Her power is low, but her interest plainly is not. Minimal monitoring would leave an engaged stakeholder without the information she is asking for, and risk turning her goodwill into frustration.

regions.label: Low power, high interest — keep informed
regions.rationale: She is highly interested and has little formal power over the project. Keeping her well informed, and using her feedback, fits both, and her knowledge of the volunteers makes that information flow valuable in both directions.

questions.explanation: Grid placement rests on two separate judgements: how much the stakeholder can affect the project, and how much they care about it. Visible engagement is evidence of interest, not of power, and confusing the two pushes vocal stakeholders into close management they cannot use. Placement is also a snapshot, so a stakeholder whose influence grows, for example through the people they represent, should be re-placed.
questions.mindset: Judge a stakeholder's power by what they can change, not by how often you hear from them.

questions.stem: You are managing an ERP replacement for a food manufacturer. The warehouse manager asked for a bespoke pallet-labelling module, and yesterday the steering committee declined it on cost grounds. The decision is recorded in minutes that will be circulated in two weeks. He is a key user whose team will run the new system every day, and he does not yet know the outcome. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Let the circulated minutes inform him in two weeks, since they record the decision and its reasoning accurately and reach every committee stakeholder at once.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it because the minutes are the formal record. But a fortnight of silence, then a line in a document, tells a key user that his request mattered less than the paperwork, and he may hear it through gossip first.

options.text: Tell him the decision and the committee's reasons in person this week, and talk through how his team's labelling will work without the module.
options.rationale: A key user whose request has been turned down should hear it promptly, directly and with the reasons, from someone who can discuss what happens next. That keeps a disappointment from becoming a grievance about how he was treated.

options.text: Ask the sponsor, who chairs the steering committee, to write to him explaining the decision so that it carries the committee's full authority.
options.rationale: Candidates pick it because the decision was the committee's. A letter from the chair adds weight but no conversation, and the practical question of how his team will now cope is one the project manager is better placed to answer.

options.text: Wait until he asks about the module, then explain the reasons and offer to raise the request again at the next funding review.
options.rationale: Waiting leaves him planning around a module that will not arrive. Offering to reopen the request also sets an expectation the committee has just declined, which candidates mistake for kindness.

questions.explanation: When a decision goes against a stakeholder, how and when they hear it shapes their engagement more than the decision itself. Tell them directly and soon, give the reasons, and move straight to what it means for them in practice. A refusal delivered by a document, or discovered by accident, turns a reasonable outcome into a breach of trust that the project then has to repair.
questions.mindset: Deliver a no to a stakeholder yourself, promptly and with reasons, before the paperwork does.

questions.stem: You are managing a council's £6 million leisure centre rebuild. Your engagement plan includes a community open day next month at which the cabinet member for leisure will present the designs to residents. The council's pre-election period begins in three weeks, and the communications officer mentions in passing that publicity involving councillors is restricted during it. The open day would fall inside that period. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Bring the open day forward by a week so that it takes place before the pre-election period begins and the cabinet member can still present.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it as a neat scheduling fix. It is decided before anyone has checked what the restrictions cover, it cuts residents' notice of the event, and a launch timed to beat the deadline can itself look like the publicity the rules exist to prevent.

options.text: Keep the open day as planned but have the project team present the designs in place of the cabinet member, so that no councillor is involved.
options.rationale: It assumes the only restriction is on councillors appearing. Pre-election rules can also limit council publicity on contested proposals, so removing the councillor may not make the event acceptable.

options.text: Ask the council's monitoring officer how the restrictions apply to the open day, and adjust the event to fit the advice given.
options.rationale: The rule belongs to someone else, and all you have is a passing summary of it. Getting the owner's interpretation first means the redesign fits what is actually restricted, which may be more or less than the summary suggests.

options.text: Postpone the open day until after the election, and tell residents that consultation on the designs will resume once the new administration is in place.
options.rationale: It is the safest option, which is why candidates pick it, but it gives up weeks of consultation the design timeline relies on without knowing whether any of it was necessary.

questions.explanation: When engagement activity runs into a rule owned by another function, whether electoral, regulatory or legal, get the owner's interpretation before redesigning the activity. Workarounds built on a second-hand summary either breach the rule in a way nobody anticipated or sacrifice engagement the rule never prohibited. The engagement plan stays the project's, but the reading of the rule does not.
questions.mindset: Before working around someone else's rule, find out from its owner what it actually says.

questions.stem: You have taken over a €40 million warehouse automation project. In your first meeting with the employee forum, an advisory body under company policy, its chair thanks you for the 'veto over the shift-pattern design' your predecessor promised them. Nothing in the engagement plan, minutes or charter mentions a veto, and the charter gives the sponsor sign-off on the shift design. The forum's cooperation is needed for the new operating model. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the chair you need to confirm what was agreed, then take it to the sponsor and return with a clear, agreed account of the forum's role.
options.rationale: The promise may or may not have been made, and either way it exceeds what the predecessor could grant. Checking, involving the person who holds the authority and then giving the forum a definite answer turns a hidden misunderstanding into an explicit agreement.

options.text: Honour the veto as the chair describes it, since the forum believes it was promised and withdrawing it now would damage the cooperation the project depends on.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it to protect the relationship. It confirms a decision right that belongs to the sponsor, on the strength of an unrecorded conversation, and stores up a worse breach for the day the sponsor overrules the forum.

options.text: Explain to the chair that the veto was not within the predecessor's gift, because sign-off on the shift design rests with the sponsor under the project charter.
options.rationale: It is accurate about authority, which is why it appeals. But it repudiates a commitment before checking what was said, and it does so alone, leaving the forum feeling the project has gone back on its word.

options.text: Say nothing about the veto for now, and involve the forum so closely in the shift design that a formal veto is unlikely ever to be tested.
options.rationale: Candidates see it as diplomatic. It leaves two incompatible understandings in place and simply hopes they never collide, which is exactly how inherited expectations turn into disputes late in a project.

questions.explanation: Commitments made to stakeholders form part of the engagement baseline whether or not anyone wrote them down, and a new project manager inherits them with the project. Establish what was actually promised, and where a promise exceeds the authority of whoever made it, resolve it openly with the person who holds that authority before giving the stakeholder an answer. Silently honouring or silently ignoring it both leave the misunderstanding in place.
questions.mindset: Treat an inherited promise as real until checked, and resolve it openly with whoever holds the authority.

questions.stem: You are managing a £22 million water pipeline for a regional utility. The route crosses a farm whose owner is in a legal dispute with the utility over compensation for an earlier scheme. Your surveyors need access to his land in five weeks. Your engagement plan assigns him to you for one-to-one contact, and he has just emailed you directly asking to meet and 'sort things out informally'. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the meeting promptly but keep the discussion to survey access, making clear at the outset that you cannot discuss the compensation dispute.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it because it keeps the relationship warm and seems careful. But the project manager cannot judge on his own what is safe to say, and the landowner may well treat access and compensation as one negotiation.

options.text: Speak to the utility's legal team before replying, and agree with them what the project can discuss with him and through which channel.
options.rationale: Anything said to a party in a live dispute can bear on that dispute, and access to his land may be entangled with it. The legal team owns that risk, so the boundaries come from them; engagement can then continue inside those boundaries.

options.text: Decline the meeting politely and pass his email to the utility's legal team, asking them to handle all further contact with him on any matter.
options.rationale: It over-routes. Legal may be content for the project to engage on access within limits, and handing every contact to lawyers turns a stakeholder the project needs into an adversary on every front.

options.text: Meet him with the land agent present and keep a written record of the discussion, so that there is a reliable account if the dispute escalates.
options.rationale: A witness and a note are sensible precautions, which is why candidates pick it, but they protect the record rather than settling the real question: whether the meeting and its content are the project's to decide at all.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder is in dispute with the organisation, the right to speak for the organisation on anything touching that dispute sits with whoever manages it. Agree the boundaries and channels with that owner first, then engage within them. The relationship need not stop, and should not if the project depends on it, but its terms are no longer the project manager's alone to set.
questions.mindset: When a stakeholder is in dispute with your organisation, agree the terms of contact with the dispute's owner before you engage.

questions.stem: You are managing the relocation of a university's chemistry department to a new building. In a private conversation, a research group leader tells you the planned move dates would interrupt a grant-funded experiment that cannot be paused without losing two years of samples. He asks you not to name him, because the dean set the dates and he fears being seen as obstructive. The dean reviews the move plan in ten days. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the conversation confidential as he asked, and encourage him to raise the clash with the dean himself before the move plan is reviewed.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it to respect his request. It leaves a two-year loss resting on the courage of the one person who has already said he will not speak, so the risk stays hidden from the person deciding.

options.text: Explain to him that a risk of this size has to be attributed, and ask for his agreement to name him when you raise it with the dean.
options.rationale: It values transparency, which is why it appeals, but attribution is not needed to manage the risk. Insisting on it teaches stakeholders that speaking privately to the project manager costs them, so the next warning never comes.

options.text: Raise the clash with the dean straight away as an urgent issue, saying that a research group has reported it, so that the dates can be reconsidered early.
options.rationale: Candidates pick it for its urgency. It skips verification, and if only one group runs such an experiment, 'a research group' names him in all but words.

options.text: Check the clash against the grant and laboratory schedules, then raise it as a move-plan risk at the review without saying where it came from.
options.rationale: Separating the information from its source lets you honour the confidence and still act. Verifying it independently also means the risk stands on evidence, so nobody needs to know who first mentioned it.

questions.explanation: Confidential input from a stakeholder can be protected and acted on at the same time by separating the substance from the source. Verify the substance independently, then put it in front of the decision-maker as a project risk. Refusing to act protects the source but hides the risk; insisting on attribution protects openness but teaches stakeholders to stop telling you things.
questions.mindset: Protect the source and still act on the information, by making the evidence carry the message.

questions.stem: Your agile team is building a journey-planning app for a rail operator. A sight-loss charity has joined as a stakeholder, and two of its members who use screen readers now attend sprint reviews. Each review consists of the team clicking through new screens on a projector while explaining them. After two reviews, the members say they could not follow and have had nothing to comment on. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send them a written summary of each review in an accessible format, so they can read what was shown and reply with their comments.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it because it solves the access problem for the meeting. But a description of screens is still second-hand, and they would be commenting on an account of the product rather than on the product.

options.text: Ask the team to describe each screen in much more detail during the demonstration, so that the members can follow it as it happens.
options.rationale: It improves the narration, which is why it appeals, but a spoken tour of a visual interface tells them nothing about how it behaves with a screen reader, which is the thing they are there to judge.

options.text: Change the review format so they can use the new features with their own screen readers, and take their feedback from that.
options.rationale: A review exists to get feedback on working product. Letting them use it the way they will use it in real life gives them something to react to, and gives the team the feedback it most needs from them.

options.text: Arrange separate accessibility testing with the charity before each release, and keep the sprint reviews in their current form for the other stakeholders.
options.rationale: Candidates pick it as a tidy split. Testing only before release means accessibility problems are found after several sprints of work, and it quietly removes these stakeholders from the event where priorities are shaped.

questions.explanation: An engagement method has to let each stakeholder contribute in the way the project needs from them. Where the purpose is feedback on a product, the method should let stakeholders experience the product as they actually would, not merely hear about it. When a stakeholder says they have nothing to comment on, check whether the format gave them anything to comment with.
questions.mindset: Design engagement around how each stakeholder can actually take part, not around how the team prefers to present.

questions.stem: An insurer's claims-portal team has become popular, and its fortnightly sprint review now draws about 45 people from across the business. The hour is spent on the demonstration, few questions are asked, and the product owner says she gets more useful feedback from corridor conversations afterwards. Several attendees value the review as their main way of seeing progress. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Limit attendance to a fixed list of named stakeholders agreed with the product owner, and ask everyone else to rely on the written sprint report instead.
options.rationale: It restores the conversation, which is why candidates choose it, but it removes the progress view that several stakeholders depend on and offers a report in its place, swapping one engagement failure for another.

options.text: Keep the review open to everyone, and split the hour into breakout groups that each look at one feature with a member of the team.
options.rationale: It keeps everyone involved and creates smaller conversations. But it scatters the feedback across tables the product owner cannot all attend, so the person deciding priorities hears least of it.

options.text: Ask attendees to send their questions in writing beforehand, so that the hour can be spent answering them rather than on the demonstration.
options.rationale: Candidates pick it to make the hour more interactive. It replaces inspection of working product with a question-and-answer session about it, which is the opposite of what a review is for.

options.text: Hold a smaller working review with the stakeholders whose feedback shapes the backlog, and share a recorded showcase with everyone else.
options.rationale: The event is trying to serve two purposes and its size is defeating one of them. Splitting them keeps the visibility the wider audience values while giving the people whose input matters a group small enough to talk in.

questions.explanation: When one engagement event is serving two purposes, such as inspecting the product with the people who shape it and giving a wider audience visibility of progress, and its size defeats the first, separate the purposes rather than giving one up. A review that has become a broadcast still informs people but has stopped producing the feedback that justifies its place in the cadence.
questions.mindset: When an engagement event outgrows its purpose, split the purposes rather than shrinking the audience.

questions.stem: Your agile team is building a reading-practice app for children aged seven to nine. Three primary schools have agreed to take part, and the product owner wants pupils to try each increment and give feedback at sprint reviews held by video call. One head teacher is keen and has offered to set up a session with her class next week. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Run the first session with the keen head teacher's class next week, and use what is learned to plan the sessions with the other two schools.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it to seize the momentum. A head teacher's enthusiasm is not the same as safeguards and consent being in place, and a pilot is still a session with real children.

options.text: Agree with each school's safeguarding lead how pupils can take part, including parental consent and how their feedback is gathered.
options.rationale: Children cannot consent for themselves, so their engagement runs through those responsible for them, under rules those people apply. Settling that first is what makes any session with pupils legitimate.

options.text: Ask teachers to try each increment as if they were pupils and report back, so that children do not need to be involved in the reviews directly.
options.rationale: It avoids the safeguarding question, which is why it appeals, but adults guessing at how seven-year-olds read is the very feedback the product owner wants to get past.

options.text: Send parents an information letter about the reviews through the schools, giving them two weeks to tell the school if they do not want their child to take part.
options.rationale: Candidates see it as covering consent. It sets the terms unilaterally, and an opt-out letter may not meet what the schools require; that judgement belongs to their safeguarding leads.

questions.explanation: When the people whose feedback you need cannot consent for themselves, such as children or adults lacking capacity, engagement runs through those who hold responsibility for them, and their rules come before the schedule. An eager gatekeeper's offer opens a door but does not put the safeguards in place. Agree the conditions of involvement first; the sessions follow from them.
questions.mindset: Settle the conditions under which vulnerable stakeholders can take part before deciding when they will.

questions.stem: A bank's agile data team has built a model that ranks suspected card-fraud cases for 60 investigators, replacing a first-in, first-out queue. Their manager supports it, but investigators are working around the ranking, saying they cannot see why cases are ordered as they are. The model performs well in testing. The product owner wants full use within two sprints. What should the project manager recommend?

options.text: Run a period in which every investigator sees the model's ranking beside their own choice of case, with disagreements fed into the backlog.
options.rationale: The distrust is spread across all 60 users, and this gives each of them evidence they can test against their own expertise, plus a visible route by which their objections change the product.

options.text: Bring two experienced investigators into the team for the next two sprints, so that the users' perspective shapes how the ranking is explained.
options.rationale: A strong option, and candidates rightly value user representation. But two colleagues' confidence does not transfer to the other 58, whose doubt rests on what they themselves cannot see.

options.text: Add a short explanation of the main factors behind each case's ranking to the investigators' screen, and train them on how to read it.
options.rationale: Explanation addresses the stated complaint, which is why candidates choose it. It still asks investigators to accept the model's reasoning rather than check it, and gives them no way to influence it.

options.text: Ask the manager to set a date after which cases must be worked in ranked order, with a channel for reporting cases that look wrongly ranked.
options.rationale: It meets the product owner's deadline and includes a feedback route, so it is defensible. But it secures compliance before trust, and investigators who doubt the tool will report less and work around it more quietly.

questions.explanation: Users who route around a tool are stakeholders telling you they have no reason to trust it. Trust in a decision aid comes from users being able to test it against their own judgement and seeing their objections change it. Representation, explanation and mandate each help, but only an arrangement that gives the whole user group its own evidence and influence addresses doubt that is held by all of them.
questions.mindset: Earn a stakeholder group's trust by letting them test the product against what they know.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme replacing a port authority's vessel-booking system, the harbour master has raised objections at each of the last three design reviews, mostly about safety checks during berthing. The sponsor, frustrated by the delays, tells you to stop inviting him to reviews and to keep him informed by monthly email instead. The harbour master signs off the operating procedures the new system will enforce. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Follow the sponsor's instruction, since she owns the programme and its schedule, and make the monthly emails detailed enough to answer his safety questions.
options.rationale: Candidates defer to the sponsor's authority. But it cuts dialogue with a stakeholder who holds a sign-off, and unresolved safety objections will return at that sign-off, later and at greater cost.

options.text: Keep inviting him to the design reviews as before, because his sign-off is needed later, and explain your reasons to the sponsor after the next review.
options.rationale: The reasoning about his sign-off is sound, which is why it appeals, but quietly overriding the sponsor and explaining afterwards damages the relationship the project manager most depends on.

options.text: Ask the sponsor what she wants the change to achieve, and propose a way of resolving the safety concerns that does not depend on excluding him.
options.rationale: The instruction is a means to an end: fewer delays. Surfacing that goal lets you offer a route to it that keeps the person whose sign-off the system needs, rather than choosing between obedience and defiance.

options.text: Meet the harbour master privately before the next review to work through his concerns, and send him the monthly updates as the sponsor directed.
options.rationale: Candidates see it as complying while limiting the harm. It works around the sponsor rather than with her, and still removes the harbour master from the forum where the design is decided.

questions.explanation: A sponsor's instruction about how to engage a stakeholder is usually a means to some other end. When following it would weaken engagement with someone whose approval the project needs, surface the conflict and offer another route to the sponsor's actual goal. Silent compliance stores up the problem; quiet defiance spends trust with the person who owns the project.
questions.mindset: When told to exclude a stakeholder, find out what the instruction is for before deciding how to respond.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is consolidating an insurer's three offices into one. The facilities director controls the floor space needed for the new training centre. In a one-to-one meeting he says he will release the space on schedule if the programme also refurbishes his own team's offices, which are outside scope and would cost about £80,000. He suggests keeping the arrangement between the two of you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree to the refurbishment provided it can be funded from the programme's contingency, since releasing the space on time protects the critical path.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it because the schedule benefit is real. But contingency is held for identified risks, not for buying cooperation, and a private side-deal on scope is exactly what change control exists to prevent.

options.text: Decline the request outright, and remind him that releasing the space is part of his role in the organisation rather than something to negotiate.
options.rationale: It is principled, which is why it appeals, but it settles alone a question that belongs to the sponsor and turns the director into an opponent while the training centre still depends on him.

options.text: Escalate his request to the sponsor as a conduct concern, so that the space can be released by instruction rather than through negotiation with him.
options.rationale: Candidates see it as routing to authority. Framing an ordinary, if awkward, request as misconduct escalates a relationship problem into a personal one and discards the chance that part of his request has merit.

options.text: Tell him you cannot agree it privately, and offer to take the refurbishment to the sponsor as a change request alongside the space dependency.
options.rationale: His support has a price attached, and the price is scope and money that the project manager does not own. Bringing both the request and the dependency into the open lets the person who does own them decide, without rejecting him.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder support that comes with conditions is a negotiation over scope and resources, and those decisions belong to whoever owns them. The project manager's job is to bring the trade into the open and put it in front of that owner, not to settle it privately in either direction. A private yes buys cooperation with money nobody approved; a private no spends a relationship the project still needs.
questions.mindset: When support comes with a price, take the price to whoever owns the budget rather than paying or refusing it yourself.

questions.stem: An online furniture retailer's agile team is building a returns-processing app. The head of customer returns is a key stakeholder whose challenges at sprint reviews have improved the product. In the last two reviews he has mocked a junior developer's work by name in front of 20 attendees, and the team has started asking to leave her features out of the demonstration. He reports to the sponsor. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Speak to him privately before the next review, say how much his challenges have improved the product, and ask him to aim criticism at the work rather than at individuals.
options.rationale: The review is a forum the project manager runs, so its norms are the project manager's to protect. A direct, private conversation keeps a valuable stakeholder engaged while correcting the behaviour that is driving work out of view.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to raise his conduct with him, since he reports to her and a correction from his own manager will carry more weight than one from you.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it because the sponsor has line authority. But it escalates before anyone has had the first conversation, and turns a fixable habit into a performance matter he may then resent the project for.

options.text: Have a senior developer present the junior developer's features at the next few reviews, so that his criticism is not aimed at someone with less experience.
options.rationale: It shields the junior developer, which is why it appeals, but it accepts the behaviour, teaches the team that work is presented by whoever can withstand ridicule, and leaves him free to do the same to the next presenter.

options.text: Replace open discussion at reviews with written feedback forms collected afterwards, so that critique reaches the team without being delivered in public.
options.rationale: Candidates see it as removing the public stage. It also removes the live discussion that made his input valuable, and penalises every attendee for one person's conduct before anyone has asked him to change.

questions.explanation: The project manager owns the forums through which stakeholders engage, including how people behave in them.
