When one stakeholder's conduct starts to distort a forum, for example by leading the team to hide work from it, address it directly with that stakeholder before escalating or redesigning the forum. A private, specific request keeps the stakeholder's contribution while removing what is doing the damage, and escalation or structural changes remain available if it does not work.
questions.mindset: Protect the forums you run by speaking directly to the stakeholder distorting them, before reaching for authority or redesign.

questions.stem: Your agile team is building a task-allocation app for a hospital's porters, commissioned by the hospital's estates manager. The porters are employed by a facilities contractor, and its site manager has refused to release any porters for usability testing, saying the contract pays only for portering hours. He was not on your stakeholder register. Testing with real porters is planned for the next sprint. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Meet the site manager to understand what releasing porters would cost his team and what the app could change for them.
options.rationale: His refusal is a position; the cost to his rota and his view of the app are the interests behind it. Finding those out is what makes a workable arrangement possible, such as short sessions at quiet times.

options.text: Add the contractor's site manager to the stakeholder register, recording that he controls the team's access to the app's users.
options.rationale: He has real influence over the project's ability to learn from its users, whether or not he will ever use the app. Recording that makes his engagement planned rather than a one-off fix.

options.text: Ask the estates manager to instruct the contractor, under the existing contract, to release porters for the planned testing sessions.
options.rationale: Candidates reach for the contractual lever because the hospital is the client. It is used before anyone knows whether the contract covers testing, and it makes the site manager an opponent for the rest of the project.

options.text: Run the usability tests with hospital staff who understand portering work, and test with the porters themselves once the app is released.
options.rationale: It keeps the sprint on schedule, which is why it appeals, but proxies cannot reveal how porters actually work, and finding that out after release is the expensive way round.

options.text: Raise the refusal with the sponsor as an impediment that is blocking the next sprint, and ask for it to be resolved at that level.
options.rationale: Candidates treat it as an ordinary impediment. Escalating a stakeholder nobody has yet spoken to skips the conversation most likely to solve it and spends senior attention on it.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder who controls access to your users is a stakeholder even if he never touches the product. When a gatekeeper blocks engagement, find out what the block is protecting before reaching for authority, and record his influence so the plan accounts for it from then on. Contractual and hierarchical levers are available later; the relationship is harder to rebuild once they have been pulled.
questions.mindset: Treat whoever controls access to your users as a stakeholder, and understand their reasons before pulling rank.

questions.stem: You are managing the consolidation of a utility's four billing centres into two, a predictive project going live in nine months. HR has begun a formal redundancy consultation with staff at the two centres that will close, and has told you that anything said about roles or timing must go through the consultation. Those staff hold most of the process knowledge your design team needs over the next three months. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree with HR which topics the project can discuss with affected staff, and how requests for their time will be made and approved.
options.rationale: The consultation is a formal process with its own owner and rules. Agreeing the boundary with HR lets the project engage these staff confidently instead of avoiding them for fear of saying the wrong thing.

options.text: Plan knowledge-capture sessions with affected staff that focus on how today's processes work, keeping away from the future structure.
options.rationale: It asks for what the design needs, current process knowledge, without touching what the consultation controls. Staff can contribute their expertise without being drawn into questions about their own jobs.

options.text: Answer staff questions about future roles honestly whenever they are asked, since evasive answers will damage their trust in the project.
options.rationale: Candidates choose it out of a commitment to openness. But HR has told you role and timing questions go through the consultation, and project answers there could prejudice a formal process.

options.text: Postpone all design work that involves affected staff until the consultation concludes, so as to avoid any risk of influencing its outcome.
options.rationale: It removes the risk entirely, which is why it appeals, but it gives up three months of design input that could have been gathered safely within agreed limits.

options.text: Use staff from the two continuing centres as the design team's main source of process knowledge, so that the consultation is not disturbed.
options.rationale: Candidates see it as a clean workaround. It ignores the fact that the knowledge sits mainly with the closing centres, and those staff may later read their exclusion as a sign of a decision already taken.

questions.explanation: When another formal process governs what can be said to a stakeholder group, engagement works within its boundaries rather than around or instead of them. Agree the boundary with the process owner, then design engagement that asks for what the project needs without touching what the other process controls. Avoiding the group altogether is as much a failure as ignoring the constraint.
questions.mindset: Work inside another process's boundaries rather than letting them end your engagement with a group.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme for a fashion retailer has finished building a new point-of-sale system with a core team of store-operations experts. The next phase rolls it out to 180 stores over eight months. Your engagement plan, written at initiation, centres on the sponsor, the store-operations experts and the IT security lead. Which two updates should the project manager make to the engagement plan before rollout begins?

options.text: Repeat stakeholder identification and analysis for the rollout phase, which brings in store managers, till staff and the support desk.
options.rationale: The people who matter during rollout are not the people who mattered during the build. A plan that still centres on the design group will miss the stakeholders whose daily work is about to change.

options.text: Schedule engagement with each store in step with its go-live date, so that staff hear from the programme shortly before the change reaches them.
options.rationale: A rollout over eight months means each store meets the change at a different time. Pacing engagement to that timing gives staff information when they can use it rather than months early or on the day.

options.text: Keep the plan as written and add a monthly rollout newsletter to every store, since the key decision-makers on the programme are unchanged.
options.rationale: Candidates assume the plan holds because the governance has not changed. But engagement covers everyone affected, and a newsletter informs without engaging the people who must now change how they work.

options.text: Ask the store-operations experts to represent all 180 stores in rollout decisions, since they understand the new system better than anyone.
options.rationale: It uses expertise the programme already has, which is why it appeals, but a handful of experts cannot speak for 180 stores' circumstances or carry their staff's concerns.

options.text: Brief all 180 store managers together at a single launch event at the start of rollout, so that every store hears the same message at once.
options.rationale: Candidates value consistency of message. A single event months ahead of most stores' go-live front-loads information and leaves later stores with nothing current when the change arrives.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder landscape depends on the phase. A plan written for design reflects who matters while the product is built; delivery to a wider population brings in new stakeholders and changes when each one needs to be engaged. Re-analysing at a phase transition, and pacing engagement to the moment each group meets the change, are part of maintaining the plan rather than optional extras.
questions.mindset: Re-identify stakeholders whenever the work moves into a phase that touches different people.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme introducing digital site diaries across a construction firm's 30 sites, three engagement needs have arisen. Match each to the person best placed to carry that engagement. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A non-executive director has questioned at board level whether the programme's benefits justify its cost.
Site foremen doubt that filling in diaries on a tablet will be quicker than paper, and are slow to start using them.
The firm's IT architect wants detail on how the diary app will exchange data with the payroll system.

options.text: The programme sponsor
options.rationale: A board-level challenge to the business case is answered by the person accountable for it, who has standing with the board and can speak to the benefits in its terms.

options.text: A foreman from a pilot site who has used the diaries for three months
options.rationale: Practical doubt about a tool is best answered by a peer who has used it on a real site. Foremen will believe someone who does their job sooner than anyone from the programme.

options.text: The programme's technical lead
options.rationale: An architect's question needs an answer that can survive detailed follow-up, which only someone who designed the integration can give.

options.text: The firm's internal communications team, through an intranet article
options.rationale: Not used. A broadcast article reaches everyone but answers none of the three specific concerns, each of which depends on the messenger's standing on that particular question.

questions.explanation: Who carries an engagement matters as much as what is said, because stakeholders weigh a message by the messenger's standing on that question. Business-case challenges go to the person accountable for the case, practical doubts are best answered by a credible peer, and technical questions by someone who can handle the follow-up. Routing every engagement through the project manager or a broadcast channel loses that standing.
questions.mindset: Choose the messenger whose standing the stakeholder will accept on that particular question.

questions.stem: You are planning stakeholder engagement for a predictive project replacing the nurse-call system across a care home group's 12 homes. Match each stakeholder to the point at which engaging them matters most. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The fire safety officer, whose approval the link between nurse-call and fire alarms will need before installation.
The external support desk that will take fault calls from the homes once the new system is live.
Residents' families, who have asked how the change will affect the way their relatives call for help.

options.text: During design, before the technical approach is fixed
options.rationale: An approver's conditions are cheapest to meet while the design is still open. Engaging the fire officer after the approach is fixed risks a redesign at the approval gate.

options.text: Ahead of go-live, while support processes and training are being prepared
options.rationale: The support desk's needs shape procedures, scripts and training, which have to be ready before the first fault call arrives on day one.

options.text: Shortly before work starts in each home, covering what will change for residents and when
options.rationale: Families need reassurance when the change is about to affect their relative. Engaging them home by home puts accurate, timely information in front of them when it matters.

options.text: At project closure, as part of the lessons-learned review
options.rationale: Not used. Closure is too late to act on any of these stakeholders' input; each one's engagement has to land before the decision or change that affects them.

questions.explanation: Each stakeholder has a point at which engagement is most valuable, usually just before the decision or change that concerns them. Engaging much earlier spends their attention on something they cannot yet use; engaging later turns input into rework and information into surprise. Plan engagement timing by mapping each stakeholder to the decision or event that touches them.
questions.mindset: Time each stakeholder's engagement to the decision or change that affects them.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is rolling out a shared maintenance system across an energy company's sites in four countries. Local norms differ in how stakeholders voice views and make decisions. Complete each sentence with the engagement response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: At one site, managers agree with every proposal in group workshops, then raise serious objections later through their regional director. The programme should
At another site, junior engineers will not commit to a design choice until the site's general manager has given a view. The programme should
Near a third site, the neighbouring community takes decisions through a monthly village assembly rather than through individual leaders. The programme should

options.text: seek each manager's views in one-to-one conversations before proposals go to a group
options.rationale: Where disagreement is not voiced in front of peers, group agreement is not evidence of support. Private conversations beforehand surface objections while they can still shape the proposal.

options.text: engage the general manager first and formally, then work through the detail with the engineers
options.rationale: Where decisions follow seniority, going to the engineers first produces stalled discussions. Securing the general manager's view gives the engineers the permission they are waiting for.

options.text: present proposals at the assembly and allow time for it to decide before acting on the outcome
options.rationale: A community that decides collectively cannot be engaged through one representative. Working to the assembly's cycle respects how its decisions are actually made and gives them legitimacy.

options.text: ask each site to nominate a single representative to a central steering forum
options.rationale: Not used. A uniform forum standardises away exactly the differences these situations describe, and would reproduce the false agreement, the stalled decisions and the missing mandate.

questions.explanation: Engagement methods have to fit how a group forms and voices its views. A method that works where people disagree openly and decide individually will produce false agreement in one place, stalled decisions in another and no mandate in a third. Observe how decisions are actually made and objections actually raised, then design the engagement around that rather than around the programme's default.
questions.mindset: Fit the engagement to how a group actually decides, not to how the programme would like it to.

questions.stem: You can give 20 hours a month to engagement on a water utility's smart-meter programme. The plan has monthly one-hour meetings with 4 key stakeholders, each needing one hour's preparation; fortnightly 30-minute calls with 6 area managers (count two per month); and a monthly 3-hour community forum. The regulator's liaison now asks for a monthly 2-hour session needing 2 hours' preparation.

blanks.label: Hours per month the current plan needs, before the regulator's session
blanks.rationale: Key stakeholders: 4 × (1 + 1) = 8 hours. Area managers: 6 × 2 × 0.5 = 6 hours. Forum: 3 hours. Total 8 + 6 + 3 = 17 hours.

blanks.label: Hours per month over the 20-hour capacity once the regulator's session is added
blanks.rationale: The regulator's session needs 2 + 2 = 4 hours, so the plan becomes 17 + 4 = 21 hours, which is 1 hour over the 20 available.

blanks.label: Total hours per month with the regulator's session added and the area-manager calls made monthly instead
blanks.rationale: Monthly calls cut the area-manager time to 6 × 1 × 0.5 = 3 hours. The plan becomes 8 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 18 hours, which fits within 20 with 2 hours to spare.

questions.explanation: An engagement plan is a commitment of finite time, and its cost includes preparation as well as contact. Costing it shows when a new stakeholder's needs can be absorbed and when they require something else to change, so the choice about which engagement to thin out is made deliberately and against priorities, rather than by quietly letting every commitment slip a little.
questions.mindset: Cost engagement in hours so that adding a stakeholder forces a deliberate choice rather than a silent overload.

questions.stem: A bus operator's agile team is replacing paper concessionary passes with a phone app. A pensioners' forum has a formal right to be consulted on changes to concessionary travel, and its members lose their paper passes when these are withdrawn in three weeks. The forum cannot halt, fund or alter the project. Select the salience-model class that describes the forum.

graphic.title: Salience model: seven stakeholder classes formed by combinations of power, legitimacy and urgency
graphic.caption: Select a class. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Dormant — power only
regions.rationale: Dormant stakeholders hold power but have no legitimate claim or pressing need. The forum has the opposite profile: a legitimate, time-critical claim and no power over the project.

regions.label: Discretionary — legitimacy only
regions.rationale: Right on legitimacy but it misses urgency. Members losing their passes in three weeks makes the forum's claim time-critical, which moves it out of this class.

regions.label: Demanding — urgency only
regions.rationale: Demanding stakeholders press a claim with no legitimate standing. The forum's formal right to be consulted gives its claim legitimacy, so this undersells it.

regions.label: Dominant — power and legitimacy
regions.rationale: The stem rules out power: the forum cannot halt, fund or alter the project. A formal right to be consulted is a right to be heard, not a power to decide.

regions.label: Dangerous — power and urgency
regions.rationale: This pairs urgency with power and no legitimacy, which is the reverse of the forum's position on two of the three attributes.

regions.label: Dependent — legitimacy and urgency
regions.rationale: A legitimate claim, a pressing deadline and no power of its own. Dependent stakeholders rely on others with power to act for them, so the project must make sure their claim reaches whoever can.

regions.label: Definitive — power, legitimacy and urgency
regions.rationale: The most common error: reading urgency as power. The forum's need is pressing, but nothing in the stem gives it the ability to change what the project does.

questions.explanation: The salience model classifies stakeholders by which of three attributes they hold: power to affect the project, legitimacy of their claim, and urgency, meaning how time-sensitive and critical the claim is. Each is judged separately, and the usual error is letting a loud or urgent claim stand in for power. Stakeholders with legitimate, urgent claims but no power depend on the project to carry their claim to those who can act on it.
questions.mindset: Judge power, legitimacy and urgency separately, and do not let urgency pass for power.
